metadata.title: Using machine learning approaches to predict Taiwanese eighth graders' computational thinking performance in ICILS 2023 study

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICILS 2023 microdata from Taiwan, with a two-stage sampling design: 169 junior high schools selected via stratified random sampling, followed by cluster sampling at the class level within selected schools. The analytic sample is restricted to Taiwanese 8th graders who completed the ICILS 2023 online questionnaire and the computational thinking (CT) performance test, with CT scores standardized by IEA using Rasch item response theory. The manuscript does not report whether ICILS sampling weights (or replicate weights) were applied in the ML training/evaluation, so the weighting approach is not transparent. Because the models are standard scikit-learn classifiers (and the paper does not describe weight-aware training), it is likely that complex survey weights were not incorporated into the predictive modeling stage; readers should treat performance metrics as conditional on the analyzed sample rather than fully population-representative estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper uses a binary classification threshold based on the mean of the first plausible value (PV1) for CT scores, but it does not describe how missing questionnaire or derived predictor values were handled before model training. This is a reporting gap because ICILS datasets typically contain non-trivial missingness across background and ICT variables, and the choice of listwise deletion vs. imputation can materially affect both model training and feature importance (e.g., SHAP). Without an explicit missing-data strategy, the stability and generalizability of the reported top predictors cannot be fully assessed.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the ICILS 2023 Taiwan dataset consisting of 8th-grade students (average age 14.3) who participated in the ICILS 2023 project and completed both the ICILS 2023 International Student Questionnaire (including the 15-item CT disposition scale embedded in the national questionnaire) and the CT performance test. The CT performance test included two randomly assigned CT modules per participant; the study then standardized CT scores using IEA Rasch scaling and converted them to a binary outcome using a PV1-based threshold (below-average vs. above-average). The manuscript reports a multi-stage feature filtering process (aggregation of overlapping/highly correlated items into derived indices, removal of variables with excessive missingness or weak theoretical connection, and VIF-based multicollinearity screening), resulting in 18 retained predictors.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Learning safe ICT use at school

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2023 Taiwan (Grade 8) Computational thinking performance (binary: below vs above average using PV1 mean threshold)
main_findings.target_variable: Computational thinking performance class (below-average vs above-average)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Best model (XGBoost): AUC=0.79, Accuracy=0.72, Precision=0.71 (below-average), Recall=0.74 (below-average), F1=0.72 (below-average); Stacking Ensemble also AUC=0.79 and Accuracy=0.72 with higher recall/F1 for above-average. Logistic Regression: AUC=0.76, Accuracy=0.69, F1=0.65 (below-average) and 0.72 (above-average).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2023 Taiwan (Grade 8) computational thinking performance the study leveraged CT disposition (CTDS), ICT self-efficacy (specialist), learning specialist classroom application, ICT self-efficacy (general), and academic media multitasking to predict computational thinking performance class (below-average vs above-average), finding that XGBoost achieved the highest overall AUC (0.79) and accuracy (0.72) and that CTDS was the most influential predictor in SHAP rankings. This indicates that strengthening students’ computational thinking dispositions and specialist ICT self-efficacy—alongside targeted classroom use of specialist applications—may improve CT achievement, though the binary PV1-based outcome and the lack of documented missing-data/weight handling limit causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes ICILS 2023 Taiwan data for 8th graders (N=5,211) using a computational thinking (CT) performance test with two randomly assigned CT modules per student. CT scores were standardized by the IEA Rasch scaling and then converted into a binary outcome (below-average vs above-average) using a PV1-based threshold (mean of PV1). The authors trained multiple supervised classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, LightGBM, XGBoost) and a Stacking Ensemble, using an 80/20 train-test split with 10-fold cross-validation on the training set. XGBoost and the Stacking Ensemble both reached AUC=0.79 and Accuracy=0.72, with XGBoost performing best overall and SHAP identifying CTDS as the top predictor. Limitations include the binary simplification of CT, reliance on PV1 for the threshold, and missing-data handling and survey-weight usage not being explicitly reported, which constrains generalizability and causal claims.
